source_text: Tempus est his decursis repetere nos de incarnatione domini et salvatoris nostri, quomodo vel homo factus est vel inter homines conversatus est. Pro viribus igitur nostris perexiguis considerata ex operum suorum magis quam ex nostri sensus contemplatione divina natura, intuitisque nihilominus creaturis eius visibilibus, fide quoque invisibilibus contemplatis, quia non omnia vel oculis videre potest humana fragilitas vel ratione conplecti, pro eo quod omnium rationabilium infirmius et fragilius animal nos sumus homines (praestantiora enim sunt ea, quae vel in caelo vel super caelos habentur): superest ut harum omnium creaturarum et dei medium, id est -mediatoremquaeramus, quem Paulus apostolus “primogenitum omnis creaturaepronuntiat. Videntes quoque nos ea, quae de eius maiestate in seripturis sanctis referuntur, et intuentes quod “imago invisibilis deie et “primogenitus omnis creaturae” dicatur, et quod “in ipso creata sunt omnia visibilia et invisibilia, sive throni sive dominationes sive principatus sive potestates, omnia per ipsum et in ipso creata sunt, et ipse est ante omnes, et omnia illi constant”, qui est “caput omnium”, solus habens “capute deum patrem, sicut seriptum est: “Caput autem Christi deus”; pervidentes etiam quod scriptum est quoniam “nemo novit patrem nisi filius, neque filium quis novit nisi pater” (quis enim potest nosse quae sib “sapientia- nisl qui genuit eam? aut quis ad liquidum quae sit ‘veritas’ novit nisi veritatis pater? quis certe universam -“verbi” sul naturam atque ipsius “dei- quae ex deo est investigare potuit nisi solus deus, -apud quem erat verbum-?): pro certo habere debemus quod hoc verbum (sive ratio dicenda est) hane sapientiam, hane veritatem nullus alius “nisi solus pater novit, de quo seriptum est: “Ne ipsum quidem mundum capere arbitror libros qui scriberentur”, de gloria scilicet et maiestate filu dei. Inpossibile namque est litteris committere ea, quae ad salvatoris gloriam pertinent. His igitur tantis ac talibus de natura filü dei consideratis, cum summa ammiratione obstupescimus quod eminens omnium ista natura ‘exinaniens’ se de statu maiestatis suae homo factus sit et inter homines conversatus sit, sicut gratia labiis eius infusa- testatur, et sicut ei testimonium reddit pater caelestis, et ut signis quoque et prodigus variisque ab eo gestis virtutibus confirmatur. Qui etiam ante praesentiam suam hane, quam ostendit in corpore, praecursores et nuntios adventus sui misit prophetas; post ascensionem vero suam in caelos sanctos apostolos divinitatis suae virtute repletos homines vel ex publicanis vel ex piseatoribus imperitos et indoctos ceircumire fecit orbem terrarum, ut ex omni gente atque ex omnibus populis piorum plebem in se credentium congregarent. 2. Verum ex omnibus de eo miraculis et magnificis illud. penitus ammirationem humanae mentis excedit, nec invenit mortalis intellegentiae fragilitas, quomodo sentire vel intellegere possit quod tanta illa potentia divinae maiestatis, ipsum illud patris verbum atque ipsa sapientia dei, in qua “creata sunt omnia visibilia et invisibilia, intra eireumseriptionem eius hominis, qui apparuit in Iudaea, fuisse credenda sit, sed et ingressa esse dei sapientia vulvam feminae et nasci parvulus et vagitum emittere ad similitudinem plorantium parvulorum; tum deinde quod et in morte conturbari refertur, ut ipse etiam profitetur dicens: “Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem”; et ad ultimum quod usque ad eam quae inter homines indignissima habetur adductus est mortem, licet post tertiam surrexerit diem. Cum ergo quaedam in eo ita videamus humana, ut nihil a communi mortalium fragihtate distare videantur, quaedam ita divina, quae nulli alii nisi illi primae et ineffabili naturae conveniant deitatis, haeret humani intellectus angustia et tantae ammirationis stupore pereulsa, quo declinet, quid teneat, quo se convertat, ignorat. Si deum sentiat, mortalem videt; si hominem putet, devicto "mortis regno cum spoliüs redeuntem a mortuis cernit. Propter quod cum omni metu et reverentia contemplandum est, ut in uno eodemque ita utriusque naturae veritas demonstretur, ut neque aliquid indignum et indecens in divina illa et ineffabili substantia sentiatur, neque rursum quae gesta sunt falsis inlusa imaginibus aestimentur. Quae quidem in aures humanas proferre et sermonibus explicare, longe vires vel meriti nostri vel ingenii ac sermonis excedit. Arbitror autem quia etiam sanctorum apostolorum supergrediatur mensuram; quin immo fortassis etiam totius creaturae caelestium virtutum eminentior est saeramenti istius explanatio. De quo nos non temeritate aliqua, sed quoniam ordo loci poposcit, ea magis quae fides nostra continet, quam quae humanae rationis adsertio vindicare solet, quam paucissimis proferemus, suspiciones potius nostras quam manifestas aliquas adfirmationes in medium proferentes. 3. lgitur unigenitus filius dei, per quem ‘omnia facta esse visibilia et invisibilia- in superioribus sermo disputationis edocuit, secundum seripturae sententiam et fecit omnia et “quae fecit diligit. Nam cum ‘invisibilis dei’ ipse sit -imago- invisibilis, participationem sui universis rationabilibus creaturis invisibiliter praebuit ita, ut tantum ex eo unusquisque participi sumeret, quanto erga eum dilectionis inhaesisset adfectu. Verum cum pro liberi arbitri facultate varietas unumquemque ae diversitas habuisset animorum, ut alius ardentiore, alius tenuiore et exiliore erga auctorem suum amore teneretur, illa anima, de qua dixit lesus quia “nemo aufert a me animam meam”, ab initio creaturae et deinceps inseparabiliter ei atque indissociabihter inhaerens, utpote sapientiae et verbo dei et veritati ac luci verae, et tota totum recipiens atque in eius lucem splendoremque ipsa cedens, facta est cum ipso principaliter unus spiritus, sicut et apostolus his, qui eam imitari deberent, promittit, quia “qui se iungit domino, unus spiritus este. Hac ergo substantia animae inter deum carnemque mediante (mon enim possibile erat dei naturam corpori sine mediatore misceri) nascitur, ut diximus, deus-homo, illa substantia media existente, cui utique contra naturam non erat corpus assumere. Sed neque rursum anima illa, utpote substantia rationabilis, contra naturam habuit capere deum, in quem, ui superius diximus, velut (m) verbum sapienti tatem tota iam cesserai. Unde et mero pro eo quod vel tota esset in fiho dei vel totum in se caperet f dei. eiiam ipsa cum ea quam assumserat carne dei filius dei virtus, Christus et dei sapiemiis ap- B pellatur; rursum dei filius, ‘per quem ommia creata sunt4 lesus Christus et; fius hominmis nomunatur. Nam et filius dei mortuus esse dieiur, pro ea seilicet natura, quae mortem wiique reeipere poterx et filus hominis appellatur, qui ‘venturus im dei patris gloria eum sanctis angelis- praedicatur. Et hae de per ommem seripturam -10 tam divina natura humanis vocabulis appellatur, quam humana natur divinae nuncupaiionis insignibus decoratur. Magis de hoe quam de ullo alio diei potest quod seriptum esi quia “erunt: ambo im earme una, et iam non sunt duo, sed earo una”. Magis enim verbum dei eum anima in carne una- esse, quam vir eum uxore putandus est. Sed et -unus spiritus- esse cum deo cui eonvenit quam hum animae. quae se ita deo per dilectionem iunxit, uf eo unus Spiritus merrio dieatur? Quod autem dilectionis en meri siisckn ndn "ete: ei inseparabilem cum deo fecerit unitatem, iia ut mom forítura fuent aui eum personae aeceptione animae eius assumptüio, sed virtutum — suarum ei merito delata, audi ad eam prophetam dicentem: “Dilexisti - iuslitüiam et; odisii iniquitatem; propterea unxit te deus, deus tuus oleo laetitiae prae participibus tuis”. Dilectionis igitur merito unguitur ‘oleo laetitiae, id est anima cum verbo dei Christus efficitur. -Unginamque ‘oleo laetitiae- non aliud intellegitur quam spiritu sancto repleri. Quod autem “prae participibus- dixit, indicat quia non gratia spiritus sicut prophetis ei data est, sed ipsius verbi dei in ea substantialis inerat “plenitudo”, sicut et apostolus dixit: “In quo inhabitat omnis plenitudo deitatis corporahter”. Denique propter hoe non solum dixit: “Dilexisti iustitiam”, sed addidit “et odisti iniquitatem”. ‘Odisse- enim ‘iniquitatem- illud est, quod scriptura dicit de eo quia “peccatum non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore eius”, et quod ait: “Temptatus per omnia pro similitudine absque peccato”. Sed et ipse dominus dicit: “Quis vestrum me arguit de peccato?” Et iterum ipse dicit de se: “Eece venit mundi huius princeps et in me non invenit quidquam”.
thought_title: Incarnation of the Lord and Savior
pass_a_gloss: It is time for us to repeat concerning the incarnation of the Lord and our Savior, how he was made man or lived among men. Therefore, considering his divine nature more from his works than from our contemplation, and also having contemplated his visible creatures, and also having contemplated his invisible creatures by faith, because human fragility cannot see all things with the eyes or comprehend them with reason, since we are the weakest and most fragile of all rational animals (for those things that are in heaven or above the heavens are more excellent): it remains for us to seek the medium of all these creatures and of God, that is, the mediator, whom the Apostle Paul calls the 'firstborn of all creation'. Also seeing those things that are referred to in the holy scriptures concerning his majesty, and contemplating that he is called the 'image of the invisible God' and the 'firstborn of all creation', and that 'all things visible and invisible were created in him and through him and for him, and he is before all things, and all things consist in him', who is the 'head of all things', having only God the Father as his head, as it is written: 'The head of Christ is God'; also foreseeing that it is written that 'no one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father' (for who can know what wisdom is, except the one who generated it? or who can know what truth is, except the Father of truth? who can investigate the nature of the Word of God, which is from God, except God alone, with whom the Word was?): we ought to hold for certain that this Word (or reason) knows this wisdom, this truth, no one else except God the Father alone, about whom it is written: 'I do not think that the world itself could contain the books that would be written', concerning the glory and majesty of the Son of God. It is impossible to commit to writing those things that pertain to the glory of the Savior. Therefore, considering these great and such things concerning the nature of the Son of God, we are astonished with the greatest amazement that this eminent nature, above all things, emptied itself from its state of majesty and was made man and lived among men, as the grace poured into his lips testifies, and as the heavenly Father bears witness to him, and as it is confirmed by the signs and wonders and various virtues done by him. He also sent prophets as forerunners and messengers of his coming before his presence, which he showed in the body; and after his ascension into the heavens, he made holy apostles, filled with his divine virtue, go around the world, men who were formerly publicans or fishermen, unskilled and uneducated, so that they might gather a people of believers from all nations and from all peoples. But of all the miracles and great deeds concerning him, that one exceeds the amazement of the human mind and does not find the fragility of mortal intelligence, how it can be believed that that great power of divine majesty, the very Word of God and the wisdom of God, in which 'all things visible and invisible were created', was enclosed within the circumference of the man who appeared in Judea, but also that the wisdom of God entered the womb of a woman and was born as a little child and emitted a cry, like the likeness of crying children; then also that it is reported that he was troubled even in death, as he himself also professes, saying: 'My soul is sorrowful even unto death'; and finally that he was led to that death, which is considered most unworthy among men, although he rose again on the third day. When therefore we see certain things in him so human that they seem not to differ from the common fragility of mortals, and certain things so divine that they suit no one else except that first and ineffable nature of divinity, the narrowness of the human intellect is stuck and is overcome by the stupor of such great amazement, so that it does not know what to decline, what to hold, or where to turn. If it perceives God, it sees a mortal; if it thinks a man, it sees one who overcame the kingdom of death and returned from the dead with spoils. On account of which, it must be contemplated with all fear and reverence, so that in one and the same thing the truth of both natures may be demonstrated, so that nothing unworthy or unseemly may be perceived in that divine and ineffable substance, nor, on the other hand, may those things that were done be estimated as false and pretended images. Which things, indeed, to bring forth into human ears and to explain in speeches, far exceed the powers or merits or genius or speech of us; but I think that it also surpasses the measure of the holy apostles; indeed, perhaps it is even more excellent than the explanation of all the celestial virtues of this sacrament. Concerning which we will bring forth not by any temerity, but because the order of the place has demanded it, those things that our faith contains, rather than what the assertion of human reason is accustomed to vindicate, with very few words, bringing forth our suspicions rather than manifest affirmations. Therefore, the only-begotten Son of God, through whom 'all things visible and invisible were made', as the scripture says, and he made all things and 'loved what he made'. For since he himself is the 'image of the invisible God', he invisibly gave a participation of himself to all rational creatures, so that each one might participate in him to the extent that he had adhered to him with love. But when, on account of the faculty of free will, there was a variety and diversity of souls, so that one was held by a more ardent love, another by a thinner and more slender love towards his author, that soul, about which Jesus said that 'no one takes away my soul from me', from the beginning of creation and afterwards inseparably and indissolubly adhering to him, as it were to the wisdom and Word of God and truth and light, and receiving all things and giving itself into his light and splendor, was made with him principally one spirit, as the apostle promises to those who ought to imitate it, that 'he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit'. Therefore, by this substance of the soul, which is a medium between God and flesh (for it was not possible for the nature of God to be mixed with the body without a mediator), the God-man is born, as we said, with this medium substance existing, to which, indeed, it was not against nature to assume a body. But neither did that soul, as a rational substance, have against nature to receive God, into whom, as we said above, it had already entirely given itself as to the Word of wisdom. Whence also, on account of this, that it was either all in the Son of God or all in itself received the Son of God, it is also called the virtue of the Son of God, Christ, and the wisdom of God; again, the Son of God, 'through whom all things were created', is called Jesus Christ, and the Son of man. For the Son of God is said to have died, on account of that nature which could receive death; and the Son of man is called the one who 'will come in the glory of God the Father with the holy angels'. And these things are called by divine names, as well as human nature is decorated with the insignia of divine nomenclature, throughout the whole scripture. It can be said more concerning this than concerning any other thing, that which is written, that 'the two will be one flesh, and they will no longer be two, but one flesh'. For the Word of God is more to be thought to be one with the soul in one flesh than a man with his wife. But also to be 'one spirit' with God is fitting for the human soul, which has joined itself to God through love, so that it may be said to be one spirit by merit. But what is the merit of love, except that it has made an inseparable unity with God, so that it is not by the assumption of the person, but by the merit of its virtues, that it is said to the prophet: 'You have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions'. Therefore, by the merit of love, it is anointed with the oil of gladness, that is, the soul with the Word of God becomes Christ. And to be anointed with the oil of gladness is understood as nothing else than to be filled with the Holy Spirit. But when it says 'beyond your companions', it indicates that it is not by the grace of the Spirit, as it was given to the prophets, but by the substantial fullness of the Word of God in it, as the apostle also said: 'In whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily'. Finally, on account of this, it did not only say: 'You have loved justice', but also added 'and hated iniquity'. For to hate iniquity is that which the scripture says concerning him, that 'he did not commit sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth', and that 'he was tempted in all things without sin'. But the Lord himself also says: 'Which of you convicts me of sin?' And again he says about himself: 'Behold, the prince of this world comes, and in me he will not find anything'.

pass_b_english: The time has come for us to return to the incarnation of the Lord and our Savior, to how he was made man and lived among men. We must consider his divine nature as best we can, drawing more from his works than from our own contemplation, and we must also look upon his visible creatures, and by faith upon the invisible ones as well. Human fragility cannot see all things with the eyes or embrace them with reason, because we humans are the weakest and most fragile of all rational animals — for those things that exist in heaven or above the heavens are more excellent. It remains, then, for us to seek the mediator between all these creatures and God, the one whom the apostle Paul calls "firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15). We also see the things spoken in the holy scriptures concerning his majesty, and we contemplate that he is called "the image of the invisible God" and "firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15), and that "in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities — all things were created through him and for him. And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:16–17). He is the "head of all things," having only God the Father as his head, as it is written: "The head of Christ is God." We also foresee that it is written: "No one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father" (Matthew 11:27). For who can know what wisdom is except the one who generated it? Or who can know what truth is except the Father of truth? Who could investigate the whole nature of the Word of God, which is from God, except God alone, with whom the Word was? We must hold it certain that this Word (or Reason) knows this wisdom, this truth — no one else but the Father alone, of whom it is written: "I do not think the world itself could contain the books that would be written" — concerning the glory and majesty of the Son of God. For it is impossible to commit to writing those things that pertain to the Savior's glory.

Having considered such great and weighty things concerning the nature of the Son of God, we are stunned with the utmost amazement that this nature, supreme above all, emptied itself from its state of majesty and was made man and lived among men. This is testified by the grace poured upon his lips, and by the heavenly Father bearing witness to him, and confirmed by the signs, prodigies, and varied virtues he performed. Even before this presence that he showed in the body, he sent prophets as forerunners and messengers of his coming. And after his ascension into the heavens, he made holy apostles, filled with the power of his divinity — men who were formerly publicans or fishermen, unskilled and unlearned — go around the whole world, so that they might gather from every nation and all peoples a godly people believing in him.

But among all his miracles and great deeds, one surpasses the amazement of the human mind entirely, and the frailty of mortal intelligence finds no way to feel or understand how it can be believed that that great power of divine majesty, the very Word of the Father and the wisdom of God, in whom "all things visible and invisible were created" (Colossians 1:16), was enclosed within the circumference of the man who appeared in Judea. And not only that, but that the wisdom of God entered the womb of a woman and was born a little child and uttered a cry, like the likeness of crying children. Then, too, it is reported that he was troubled even in death, as he himself professes, saying: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." And finally, that he was led to that death which is considered most unworthy among men, although he rose again on the third day. When therefore we see certain things in him so human that they seem to differ in nothing from the common frailty of mortals, and certain things so divine that they suit no one else but that first and ineffable nature of divinity, the narrowness of the human intellect is caught and pierced through with the stupor of such great amazement, so that it does not know what to reject, what to hold, or where to turn. If it perceives God, it sees a mortal; if it thinks him a man, it sees one who conquered the kingdom of death and returned from the dead with spoils. On account of this, he must be contemplated with all fear and reverence, so that in one and the same person the truth of both natures may be demonstrated — so that nothing unworthy or unseemly may be perceived in that divine and ineffable substance, nor, on the other hand, may the things that were done be judged as false and pretended images. To bring these things into human ears and explain them in speech far exceeds our powers, or merits, or genius, or speech. I think it even surpasses the measure of the holy apostles; indeed, perhaps the explanation of this sacrament is more excellent than that of all the celestial virtues of creation. Concerning this we will speak not by any temerity, but because the order of the place demanded it — those things that our faith contains, rather than what the assertion of human reason is accustomed to vindicate — in very few words, putting forward our suspicions rather than manifest affirmations.

Therefore, the only-begotten Son of God, through whom "all things were made, visible and invisible" (Colossians 1:16), as the scripture says, both made all things and "loved what he made." For since he himself is the "image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15), he invisibly gave a participation of himself to all rational creatures, so that each might participate in him to the extent that he had adhered to him with the affection of love. But when, on account of the faculty of free will, variety and diversity of souls arose, so that one was held by a more ardent love, another by a thinner and more slender love toward his author — that soul, about which Jesus said, "No one takes my soul from me," from the beginning of creation and thereafter inseparably and indissolubly adhering to him, as to the wisdom and Word of God and truth and true light, and receiving all things and yielding itself into his light and splendor, was made with him principally one spirit, just as the apostle promises to those who ought to imitate it: "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit." Therefore, by this substance of the soul mediating between God and flesh (for it was not possible for the nature of God to be mixed with the body without a mediator), the God-man is born, as we said, this mediating substance existing — to which it was certainly not against nature to assume a body. Nor did that soul, as a rational substance, have it against its nature to receive God, into whom, as we said above, it had already entirely given itself as to the Word of wisdom. Whence also, on this account — that it was either wholly in the Son of God or wholly received the Son of God in itself — it is also called the power of the Son of God, Christ, and the wisdom of God; again, the Son of God, "through whom all things were created" (Colossians 1:16), is called Jesus Christ, and the Son of man. For the Son of God is said to have died, on account of that nature which could receive death; and the Son of man is called the one who "will come in the glory of the Father with the holy angels." And these things are called by divine names throughout the whole scripture, just as human nature is decorated with the insignia of divine nomenclature. More can be said of this than of any other thing: that which is written, "The two shall become one flesh, and they shall no longer be two, but one flesh." For the Word of God is more to be thought one with the soul in one flesh than a man with his wife. But also to be "one spirit" with God is fitting for the human soul which has joined itself to God through love, so that it may be said to be one spirit by merit. But what is the merit of love, except that it has made an inseparable unity with God — so that it is not by the assumption of the person, but by the merit of its virtues, that it is said to the prophet: "You have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions" (Psalm 45:7). Therefore by the merit of love it is anointed with the oil of gladness — that is, the soul with the Word of God becomes Christ. And to be anointed with the oil of gladness is understood as nothing else than to be filled with the Holy Spirit. But when it says "beyond your companions," it indicates that it is not by the grace of the Spirit as it was given to the prophets, but by the substantial fullness of the Word of God in it, as the apostle also said: "In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:9). Finally, on account of this, it did not only say "You have loved justice," but added "and hated iniquity." For to hate iniquity is that which the scripture says concerning him: "He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth," and that "he was tempted in all things like as we are, yet without sin." But the Lord himself also says: "Which of you convicts me of sin?" And again he says of himself: "Behold, the prince of this world comes, and in me he will find nothing."
